headline: Massachusetts Question 6 would steer existing sales-tax revenue to conservation
dek: The Nov. 3 referendum would create a Nature for All Fund, but the money would come from existing state tax receipts and still require legislative appropriations.
body: Massachusetts voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to create a state Nature for All Fund, a proposal that would dedicate part of the sales-tax revenue already collected on sporting goods, recreational vehicles and golf courses to land, water and outdoor-recreation projects. Question 6 is one of nine binding statewide questions on the 2026 ballot. The official voter guide from the [Massachusetts Secretary of the Commonwealth](https://www.sec.state.ma.us/divisions/elections/research-and-statistics/2026-ballot-questions.htm) says the measure would take effect July 1, 2027.

The proposal is structured as a gradual earmark rather than a new tax. During the fund’s first year, it would receive 50% of the covered tax receipts, subject to legislative appropriation. Beginning July 1, 2028, it would receive 100% of those receipts, again subject to appropriation. The ballot summary says the calculation excludes money already transferred to the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority State and Local Contribution Fund and the School Modernization and Reconstruction Trust Fund.

That distinction is the central budget question. A yes vote would not raise the sales-tax rate on a pair of hiking boots, a fishing rod, a recreational vehicle or a round of golf. It would reserve an existing stream of revenue for a specified purpose. The state’s official fiscal statement says the measure would divert tens of millions of dollars now supporting the operating budget and would carry substantial implementation costs. The statement also says a full fiscal analysis was not feasible, so the eventual amount is not presented as a fixed annual appropriation.

Independent estimates help explain why the numbers vary. Supporters cited by [WBUR](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/06/massachusetts-question-6-ballot-environment-parks-land-water) say the fund could receive more than $100 million a year. The nonpartisan Tufts Center for State Policy Analysis estimates a fully phased-in earmark of about $65 million and says Massachusetts currently spends roughly $400 million annually on recreation and conservation. Those figures describe different assumptions about the taxable base and the way the earmark would operate; neither is a guarantee of what lawmakers would ultimately spend.

The eligible uses are broad but defined. The ballot language includes protecting drinking-water supplies, streams, rivers, lakes, coasts, farms and forests; preserving connections between open spaces; and protecting lands and natural resources of Indigenous cultural significance. It also covers creating, improving and managing parks, trails, greenspaces and access to outdoor recreation. State agencies, cities and towns, public charities working in conservation, tribal governments and other regional public entities could receive money from the fund.

Question 6 would also establish a 15-member Nature for All Board. Five members would be state officials and 10 public members would be appointed by the governor. The public seats would be required to include representatives of underserved communities and Indigenous peoples, along with at least one person with conservation experience. The board would set rules for spending, including standards tied to environmental justice, Indigenous cultural resources and affordable-housing development, while the Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs would administer the fund.

Supporters frame the measure as a way to make conservation funding more predictable as climate pressure, development and deferred maintenance compete for state attention. WBUR reported that outdoor recreation generated $14.6 billion for the Massachusetts economy and supported more than 100,000 jobs in 2024. The Nature for Massachusetts coalition, which supports Question 6, includes more than 100 businesses and organizations. Those economic figures show why the proposal reaches beyond hikers and conservation groups, but they do not prove that an earmark would produce a particular number of jobs or projects.

The official voter guide says there was no organized opposition committee when it was printed, but it includes a state-prepared argument against the question. That argument warns that permanently earmarking up to all of the covered receipts could reduce budget flexibility and displace other state priorities. It also emphasizes that the Legislature retains exclusive authority over appropriations. In practical terms, passage would create the legal framework and a dedicated account, but lawmakers would still control yearly spending decisions.

The choice facing voters is therefore less about whether Massachusetts should conserve land and water than about how that work should be financed and governed. A yes vote would create a dedicated conservation mechanism beginning in 2027; a no vote would leave the existing system of general revenue, bonds and annual budget decisions in place. The official guide, including the full summary and fiscal language, is available through the [Secretary of the Commonwealth’s 2026 ballot-question page](https://www.sec.state.ma.us/divisions/elections/research-and-statistics/2026-ballot-questions.htm).
